entities.summary:
Carnegie Hall in New York City is the most prestigious concert hall in the Western Hemisphere and one of the world's most recognized venues for classical music, opened on May 5, 1891 with Pyotr Tchaikovsky conducting. Financed by industrialist Andrew Carnegie as a gift to New York City, Carnegie Hall has hosted virtually every major classical musician, jazz artist, and popular performer of the 20th century — 'to play Carnegie Hall' is the most widely understood shorthand for achieving musical excellence in American culture.

The hall was designed by architect William Burnet Tuthill with advice from conductor Walter Damrosch, who campaigned Carnegie to fund it. The 2,804-seat main auditorium (Stern Auditorium) is renowned for acoustics so exceptional that the surface of the hall cannot be altered without creating acoustic committees. Tchaikovsky conducted the opening concert; subsequent performers include Gustav Mahler, Arturo Toscanini, Leonard Bernstein, Maria Callas, Judy Garland, Frank Sinatra, the Beatles (1964), Billie Holiday, and virtually every major classical and popular artist of the past century.

Carnegie Hall was almost demolished in 1960 to make way for an office tower until violinist Isaac Stern organized a preservation campaign, saving it as a city landmark. The 1986 and 2003 renovations restored and improved the acoustic shell. Carnegie Hall's international footprint includes music education programs, the Carnegie Hall Archives (over 100,000 items), and the Weill Music Institute serving 75,000 students annually in New York.
